authors: Eichenauer, V. Z.; Köppl, S.; Köppl-Turyna, M.
title: Investment screening and venture capital
venue: EcoAustria Research Paper No. 30 (also Kiel Working Paper 2282 / CESifo WP 11538)
method: panel regressions on cross-border VC deals (Preqin) linked to country-sector screening coverage (PRISM data extended by Eichenauer & Wang), Europe 2007-2022
outcomes: number, size and structure of cross-border venture capital deals
headline: Despite very few deals actually being blocked, the spread of investment screening is associated with a significant decline in cross-border VC deals in Europe, strongest for financial investors, late-stage rounds and non-OECD investors.
summary_plain: When European countries started checking foreign investments for security risks, fewer foreign venture capital investors put money into European start-ups, even though almost no deals were actually stopped.
quality: Panel design exploiting staggered national screening reforms; measures national regimes around the EU framework rather than Regulation 2019/452 alone; exact effect sizes not in abstract

authors: Kaya, O.; Mostowfi, M.; Sugandhita, S.
title: Foreign investment screening and cross-border M&A in sensitive sectors: Evidence from Germany
method: difference-in-differences on firm-level M&A data (newly regulated vs other sectors), Germany 2016-2024
outcomes: likelihood and type of foreign acquisitions of German firms by investor origin
headline: Germany's 2020 screening reform significantly raised the likelihood that German firms in newly regulated sectors were acquired by investors from other EU countries, driven by majority-control deals, shifting ownership from non-EU to EU investors.
summary_plain: After Germany tightened checks on foreign takeovers in sensitive sectors in 2020, more of these firms were bought by investors from other EU countries rather than from outside the EU.
quality: Clean DiD on national reform that coincided with and partly implemented the EU framework (AWG/AWV 2020 amendments); single-country, effect sizes not in abstract

title: Mystery Shopping Survey on territorial restrictions and geo-blocking in the European Digital Single Market (MSS 2019) - Executive summary
venue: Publications Office of the EU, doi:10.2873/148672
method: mystery shopping measurement study: 8,976 paired domestic/cross-border website evaluations across EU28 (Oct-Dec 2019), compared with identical 2015 survey
outcomes: website access, product availability, registration, delivery, price differentiation, payment restrictions for cross-border shoppers
headline: Cross-border registration failure fell from 26.9% (2015) to 14.0% (2019) and price differentiation fell 2.3 points to 27.2%, but only 35.6% of websites let cross-border shoppers buy like locals (+0.5 points) and 53.1% did not deliver to the shopper's country.
summary_plain: A year after the ban, online shops blocked foreign shoppers less often at registration and charged them different prices a bit less often, but most shops still would not deliver abroad, so overall the chance of buying from another country barely changed.
quality: Large before/after measurement with identical method, no control group; delivery is outside the Regulation's scope; executive summary read

authors: Basalisco, B.; Salmaso, E.; Marquardt, G.; Ballebye Okholm, H.; Kotiranta, J.; Abecasis, P.; Kleberg, S. W.; Graef, I.; Monti, G. (Copenhagen Economics)
title: Study for further evaluation of the geo-blocking regulation
venue: Study for the European Commission, DG CNECT; Publications Office, doi:10.2759/89415
method: survey of 2,800+ e-commerce firms in ten EU countries, descriptive analysis of Euromonitor/Eurostat cross-border e-commerce data 2016-2022, stakeholder interviews
outcomes: cross-border e-commerce volumes and shares, barriers reported by traders, compliance
headline: Stakeholders report high compliance with the geo-blocking ban, but cross-border origin e-commerce rose only from 20% (2016) to 22% (2021) of EU e-commerce and traders and consumers say the ban had no significant effect on cross-border trade volumes.
summary_plain: Shops mostly stopped blocking foreign customers, but people did not buy much more from other EU countries; delivery costs, VAT rules and differing national rules still hold cross-border online shopping back.
quality: Descriptive trends plus large firm survey; COVID-19 shock confounds trends; no counterfactual
interested_party: Commissioned by the European Commission (DG CNECT)

authors: EBA, EIOPA & ESMA (Joint Committee of the ESAs)
title: 2025 Report on major ICT-related incidents (JC 2026 16)
venue: Joint-ESA report under Article 22 of DORA
method: descriptive statistics on all major ICT incident reports filed under DORA in 2025
outcomes: number, type, root cause, cross-border reach and impact of major ICT incidents
headline: Financial entities reported 3,383 major ICT incidents in 2025 (0.18 per entity), mostly in credit and payments; about one third had cross-border impact, almost one third originated from third parties, and two thirds caused no or minor client disruption.
summary_plain: The first year of DORA's incident reporting shows thousands of serious IT incidents in EU finance, mostly at banks and payment firms, often caused by outside IT suppliers, though most had little effect on customers.
quality: Census of mandatory reports but first year, divergent reporting practices, ~15% of incidents excluded for missing final reports; no pre-DORA baseline

title: DORA European Survey - 2025 edition
method: survey of financial entities (CISOs, CROs, DORA programme managers) in 28 countries, early 2025; sample size not stated on landing page
outcomes: self-assessed compliance by DORA pillar, expected compliance spending, hardest tasks
headline: Only 25% of entities felt compliant on ICT risk management and 8% on resilience testing and third-party risk; 64% plan to spend EUR 2-5 million on DORA compliance and 46% find the register of information the hardest task.
summary_plain: Just after DORA started applying, most financial firms surveyed said they were not yet fully compliant and expected to spend several million euros each to get there.
quality: Self-reported, sample size and selection unknown; full report gated behind registration

title: Europe's new resilience regime: The race to get ready for DORA
method: survey of major European financial institutions and critical ICT third-party providers (as of April 2024); sample size not stated
outcomes: implementation progress, staffing, expected run costs, confidence in meeting deadline
headline: Only about a third of financial institutions were confident of meeting all DORA requirements by January 2025, and 70% said continued compliance would permanently raise technology run costs.
summary_plain: Six months before DORA applied, most large financial firms had started preparing, but only one in three expected to be fully ready on time and most expected lasting extra IT costs.
quality: Pre-application readiness survey, unknown sample, self-reported; early-implementation evidence only

authors: National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC)
title: European Union CyberTipline Data Snapshot (2020 vs 2021) and updates on the ePrivacy Directive
method: before/after descriptive comparison of CyberTipline reports resolving to EU countries around the Dec 2020 ePrivacy (EECC) change and the Aug 2021 interim derogation
outcomes: number of CSAM reports and files referred to EU countries
headline: EU-related CyberTipline reports fell 47% (1,046,350 to 555,831) and files 58% between 2020 and 2021, while global reports rose 35%; NCMEC reported a 58% drop in the 18 weeks after 21 Dec 2020, before the derogation applied.
summary_plain: When the legal basis for scanning private messages lapsed in late 2020, reports of child abuse material linked to the EU fell sharply, which advocates cite as evidence of what the temporary derogation preserves.
quality: Simple before/after, confounded (e.g. Meta stopped Messenger scanning in the EU for most of 2021); mostly measures the gap before the Regulation applied, i.e. the counterfactual
interested_party: Campaigning NGO (advocated adoption of the derogation)

title: Processing under EU Regulation 2021/1232 (EU CSAM Derogation report 2025, covering 2024)
method: provider transparency report required by Art. 3(1)(g)(vii): counts of detections, appeals and reversals for hash-matching on Messenger and Instagram Direct
outcomes: CSAM detections, user appeals, error (overturn) rate
headline: Meta actioned about 1.5 million pieces of CSAM media in EU-related private message threads in 2024; about 76.9 thousand were appealed and 1.8 thousand restored, an overturn rate of 0.12%.
summary_plain: Meta says its automatic matching of known abuse images in private messages involving EU users flagged about 1.5 million items in 2024, and only about one in a thousand was later found to be a mistake.
quality: Self-reported by a firm subject to the act, not audited; overturn rate understates errors (only appealed cases)

title: Large scale EU customs control action shows most third-country e-commerce goods do not follow standards (results of priority control area action and product compliance controls report 2022-2024)
venue: European Commission, Taxation and Customs Union news, 7 January 2026
method: EU-wide customs priority control action (20,000 toys and small electronics checked, sample lab-tested) plus Member State statistics on customs product-compliance controls under Art. 25 of Regulation 2019/1020, 2022-2024
outcomes: non-compliance of imported e-commerce goods; customs interventions and refusals
headline: More than half of 20,000 checked e-commerce toys and small electronics did not meet EU standards and 84% of lab-tested items were dangerous, while customs refused on average only 13 items per million released in 2024 as controls lag e-commerce growth.
summary_plain: Border checks show most cheap products shipped directly to EU shoppers break EU safety rules, but customs can only stop a tiny fraction of the billions of parcels arriving.
quality: Official monitoring data; targeted (risk-based) sample so non-compliance not representative; underlying report not opened, read via Commission news page
interested_party: Commission reporting on its own framework
